Went straight here after a 6-hour drive last night and the service was impressive right from the start. Even though it was packed at around 9:40 PM, we were seated right away. Banchan (appetizers) came out immediately, and ordering was quick and efficient.

I ordered the beef back rib soup, and it absolutely hit the spot—rich, comforting, and loaded with meat. At around $25, it’s great value and easily a 5/5 for both taste and price.

My partner ordered the beef hot plate stew with cheese, which was over $100. Unfortunately, that dish didn’t live up to the price. It was heavy on vegetables and bones, and while the flavor was okay (a bit on the sweet side), it just didn’t feel worth it. I’d rate it 2/5 for taste, but 0/5 for value.

Atmosphere wasn’t great—busy, loud, and not very relaxing (2/5). But the service really stood out (5/5).

Atmosphere: 2/5

The restaurant has a warm, bustling feel that makes it perfect for late‑night cravings or group meals.

Seating can be tight, but the energy of the space adds to the overall experience. The menu leans heavily toward meat dishes, so it’s ideal for diners who enjoy hearty Korean comfort food. Despite the crowds, the service remains attentive, and dishes come out consistently well‑prepared.

Overall, Sun Nong Dan is a place you remember long after the meal, especially if you enjoy Korean cuisine with strong flavors and generous portions. It’s the kind of restaurant you naturally return to whenever you’re craving something warm, bold, and comforting.

Reviewers complaining about price are ignorant of the extremely generous breakfast special? This restaurant has nourished me many times over the years with their breakfast special and complimentary hot tea. It feels generous and like the restaurant is giving back to the community.

Service is great, though especially so from Jayden and Brian, whom I’m always glad to see during the day shifts. They’re always kind and patient and attentive, even when the restaurant is very busy as it is often.

The soups themselves are flavorful and taste good quality. The tta roh guk bap is especially seasoned and delicious. The rice is always good too.

This morning I got the traditional seolangtang whose calming plainness balances very well with the seasoned banchan.

text.text:
After a long, wonderful day exploring LACMA and Hollywood, my friends and I wanted to end our last evening in LA on a high note—and BCD seemed like the perfect spot for our first authentic Korean dining experience. We arrived around 11 PM, ready for a feast, but immediately noticed a long line of guests waiting outside.

We put our name down and settled in for a 30-minute wait. While standing there, I couldn't help but notice that a significant portion of the restaurant sat empty, with used dishes still left uncleared from earlier seating. I totally understand that closing off a section might be due to a short-staffed kitchen or closing procedures (especially that late!), but it was a bit puzzling to see such a long queue out front while tables sat uncleaned and unused inside. A little transparency or a quick heads-up from the hostess would have gone a long way.

That said, once we were finally seated, the food completely made up for it! We ordered quite the feast—the LA Galbi Combo, Spicy Pork Bulgogi, and Chicken Teriyaki Combo. Every dish came with generous sides of Soon Tofu Soup, Hot Pot Rice, and a beautiful array of traditional Korean banchan. The flavors were rich, comforting, and absolutely worth the hype for a first-timer like me.

Overall, the meal itself was fantastic, and the service after we sat down was efficient. Just be prepared for a potential wait if you're coming late at night, even if the restaurant looks partially empty—hopefully, they can work on clearing tables faster to reduce that bottleneck. Would still recommend for the delicious food!

Visited BCD Tofu House in LA Koreatown, and this place is basically a must-visit if you’re craving authentic Korean food.

The soft tofu stew (soondubu) is the star here — rich, spicy, and full of flavor. It comes out boiling hot, and you can really customize the spice level and ingredients to your taste.

What I really liked is the side dishes (banchan). They keep refilling them, and the quality is solid across the board. The fried fish that comes with the meal is also a nice bonus.

The place is open late (some locations are even 24 hours), so it’s perfect for late-night meals or after drinks. That’s probably why it’s always busy.

The vibe is casual and a bit hectic, but that’s part of the experience. Service is fast and efficient.

Overall, if you want a real Korean dining experience in LA, this place delivers. Simple, satisfying, and consistently good.

We gather around a steaming bowl of soft tofu soup, sharing stories, prayers, laughter, and the little moments of everyday life.

Sometimes I think people in their 60s and 70s are a lot like soft tofu. We may look gentle on the outside, but we’ve been shaped by years of love, sacrifice, faith, and perseverance. Like a hot stone pot, each of us carries a life story that has been slowly simmering over time.

Good food brings us together, but meaningful conversations are what keep us coming back. Every breakfast here fills not only our stomachs but also our hearts.

Highly recommended for anyone looking for authentic Korean comfort food and a warm place to connect with people. ❤️

text.text:
The Best Kimchi!

I think this place is known for their bossam dish, but I actually haven’t tried it yet. What keeps me coming back is their fresh napa kimchi — it’s crisp, refreshing, and incredibly flavorful.

The dolsot bibimbap is good too, though I wish the rice at the bottom was crispier to give it that deeper toasted texture and contrast.

I’d say stay away from the mandoo guk, though. It’s not seasoned properly at all. The broth is overly salty, the meat is overcooked to the point where most of the flavor is gone, and the dumplings don’t taste fresh — they seem frozen. The dumpling filling is actually overseasoned, which clashes even more with the salty broth. The whole dish falls apart because the flavors don’t complement each other. It feels like there wasn’t much thought put into balancing the broth with the dumplings and glass noodles.

What more can I say? This K-town staple consistently delivers when you're craving Korean cuisine. We started our meal with a generous portion of Haemool Pajeon (Seafood Pancake), which arrived sizzling on a hot plate reminiscent of a Chili's Fajita Plate. Next came the main attraction: the Bossam Plate, featuring simmered and cooled pork belly sliced to perfection. When you wrap all the other ingredients together, they create the perfect bite. Just after the Bossam Plate hits the table, a bubbling cauldron of Kimchi JJigae (Kimchi Stew) follows behind just in time to help wash down the delectable bites of bossam. Don't forget to order some rice because you'll need something to soak up the stew which turns the rice into a whole meal by itself.

The service was jovial and welcoming, and like other Korean establishments, they have a handy-dandy button that jolts the attention of every server working whenever you're in need of service. The small space is very cozy, just the way I like it when I'm visiting with my loved ones. They don't have an extensive menu, just the OG staple items, but I feel the taste has improved over the years. I wish Kobawoo were closer to where I live, or I would be here this weekend, but perhaps it's a good thing we're so far apart.

First time to Anju House it very much has an "house" feel with cute and chill décor with in and out seating.  I went there around 6pm and did not have an issue finding street parking, but I could see it being an issue later in the night.  When I initially entered in, there was no one at the front desk so I waited....and waited...and waited.  After about 10 minutes, I walked into restaurant and found a server.  He said that when it's not busy, no one really mans the front desk.  I guess customers are supposed to just know to walk into the back.  Very strange.  As for the menu, I was very happy with the food options.  It had so many things that I liked or sounded interesting.  What wasn't happy were the prices.  The prices are high considering portion size.  Like really high.  The prices for the "Small Anju" dishes seem reasonable, until you see the portion size.  The "Big Anju" are regular sized dishes that are very expensive.  Like, how do these young people ( a definite younger crowd that comes in later in the night) afford to eat out at places like this?  Order one or two dishes and share?

I ordered the Spicy Seafood Udon, Spicy Korean Fried Chicken, and the Fried Rice Cakes and Sausage.  The Spicy Seafood Udon was good, but nothing unique.  The Spicy Korean Fried Chicken was very well seasoned and tasty.  The Fried Rice Cakes and Sausage was just okay.  I felt that it needed more sauce and have had much better at other places.  I would be interested in trying some of the other dishes, but considering the prices, I would hesitate to come back.  The food wasn't extraordinary enough for me to ignore the prices.

Overall, I wouldn't be opposed to going back, but not my first option.

Taylor’s Steak House had been on my Los Angeles steakhouse bucket list for a while, and I’m glad I finally made it. The moment I walked through the door, I knew I had found exactly the classic old-school steakhouse atmosphere I was looking for. No gimmicks, no trendy concepts—just a traditional steakhouse focused on good food, strong drinks, and a relaxed dining experience.

We ordered the New York Strip, the 20 oz Ribeye, and a Caesar Salad. The steaks were the highlight of the meal: quality cuts, cooked well, full of flavor, and served in generous portions. The Ribeye in particular was rich, juicy, and satisfying. Service was attentive and friendly without being overbearing, which fit perfectly with the laid-back vibe of the restaurant.

The Caesar Salad was decent, although the lettuce could have been fresher. It wasn’t a deal breaker, but it was the one part of the meal that didn’t quite match the quality of the steaks.

Another pleasant surprise was the pricing. For the quality, portion sizes, and overall experience, Taylor’s offers excellent value compared to many steakhouses in Los Angeles.

Overall, this was a great experience and the first item officially checked off my LA steakhouse bucket list. If you’re looking for a classic, no-nonsense steakhouse with quality meat, reasonable prices, and a genuinely comfortable atmosphere, Taylor’s is easy to recommend. I’ll definitely be back to work my way through more of the menu.

Been here twice without reservations, first time we were sat at a booth right away, second time we were told the wait would be about 2.5 hours unless we were willing to sit at the bar, once at the bar for 10 minutes or so we got offered a small table in the back.

We were sat next to a loud family and the servers apologized to us about it even tho we never complained or minded it.

The steaks are cooked and seasoned perfectly. We've had the Kansas Steak, Spencer steak and the thick cut prime rib (great but not our preferred meat) .

The sides have all been good, we've tried the mashed potatoes(so simple yet so so satisfying), French onion soup, filet mignon chili, crispy fried onions, baked potato & sauteed garlic spinach.

The berry mojito was amazing the first time and sadly not great the second visit 🤧.

The red velvet cake was nothing special just ok, kinda giving grocery store cake, the key lime pie was good.

Parking is valet in the back of the restaurant for $5.50 but they will pocket your change and tip themselves without asking. Gave $10 and didn't get change when they only drive your car a few feet away to park it themselves. 🧍🏻‍♀️ Kinda weird and entitled in my opinion, We just spent $200 + tip inside and then have to tip on top of parking for parking. 🧍🏻‍♀️

Hands down the best Korean comfort food out here. My wife and I decided to hit up this spot after craving some Korean food on a hot day. Parking is valet ($4-5) but we decided to park across the plaza in H Mart and walked over.

We waited in line for about 5 minutes but the staff brought out menus for us to order in advance. When we got seated, we got our food pretty quickly, about 10 minutes or so, which is pretty quick because the restaurant was full and super busy.

We ordered the Medium Bossam (Feeds 1-2 people), and the MILMYON (Cold noodles) and my goodness the milmyon is beyond amazing. The noodle is different from other restaurants that serve milmyon. Their noodles mixed super well with the ingredients and it was very savory, amazing on a hot day.

The bossam came after the milmyon and the portions are pretty generous. Medium serves 1-2 people and it's very fulfilling. It's recommended to eat the bossam wrapped style but eating it piece by piece is also very tasty. The wrap ingredients matches really well and a must try for anyone visiting Hangari.

Overall, an amazing experience, wait wasn't too long despite the line. Staff were professional and fast. Food is top quality and very very tasty. This is absolutely hands down the best milmyon ever and the bossam is definitely top quality. Will be coming back often for the other dishes.

Visited Hangari Kalguksu on a cold, rainy Thursday afternoon, and the cozy atmosphere immediately gave us a sense of comforting warmth. We were promptly seated and welcomed with complimentary warm corn silk tea, which had a smooth texture and subtle sweet-corn flavor — perfect for the chilly day.
The banchan (complimentary side dishes) and sauces were well-fermented with a pleasant saltiness that paired nicely with the overall meal. For appetizers, we ordered the medium Bossam with the pork having a great balance between lean meat/fat, and when wrapped with garlic, jalapeños, spicy radish, and lettuce, it had a flavorful and satisfying taste.
The Spicy Seafood Kalguksu featured a rich, anchovy-based broth that was warmly spiced without being overpowering. The house-made knife-cut noodles were perfectly cooked having a nice chewiness. The barley rice topped with bean paste was also a great complement to the soup.
We also tried the Hot Stone Bibimbap, which arrived in a sizzling hot bowl. The vegetables, beef, and spicy gochujang sauce blended well together, and the crispy rice at the bottom added great texture.
Service was average but pleasant — the staff was approachable and attentive, checking in when needed and promptly clearing dishes.
Overall, despite the day trip it took us to get there, we’d recommend this spot to anyone looking for authentic Korean comfort food in Koreatown.

This restaurant is best known for its meat dishes, but I came by during lunch to try their lunch combo and burger specials.

Normally, when we come here for barbecue, it’s a serious commitment. The last time five of us ate here and really went all out on the meat, the bill was close to $1,000. This time, though, my friend and I stopped by for a lighter lunch.

The cold noodles were delicious, and the meat was excellent as always. We also ordered dessert afterward. It was really good, but the price definitely made me do a double take—and it disappeared in just a few bites!

The restaurant was packed, so it was quite noisy throughout the meal. Still, I can’t complain too much because the food was genuinely satisfying.

Overall, despite the crowds and the premium prices, we had a very enjoyable meal and left in a good mood.

text.text:
Friends took us here for a birthday dinner — a party of eight. It was my first visit to Park’s BBQ, one of those highly hyped Koreatown institutions: packed dining room, long waiting line, clearly no shortage of customers.

Let me start with the best part: the food was good.

The meats and sides were generous, everything tasted good, and our check of around $500 for eight people struck me as very reasonable considering the amount and quality of meat we had.

Would I go back?
Absolutely not.

A word about my ratings, because this probably matters here:
By default, every restaurant has three stars. If it were less, I would not go in the first place. Everything above three needs to be earned. If I am pleasantly surprised, it is four stars. If I am willing to make a 30-minute detour at any time just to go there, it is five stars — and only then.

So yes: good food, a clean environment and competent, friendly service are three-star territory for me.

That's the DEFAULT setting for me.

They are what I expect when I choose to eat at a restaurant, not something I consider extraordinary.

At Park’s, the service was friendly, but not particularly caring, and the entire evening felt rushed. The meats were presented at such a pace that it increasingly felt less like dinner and more like an exercise in getting the table turned. And apparently it worked.

Our birthday dinner for eight was over in approximately 75 minutes.
For a $500 dinner celebrating someone’s birthday, that is not remotely the experience I am looking for.

Then there is the noise.

I understand that Korean barbecue restaurants are lively. I am not expecting candlelight and whispered conversation. But this was something else entirely. It appeared that very little thought had been given to noise reduction. The restaurant was so loud that we could barely have a conversation with the person sitting directly opposite us. I was seated in the middle of our table and communicating with anyone toward either end was practically impossible. Again: there were eight of us, not twenty.

And then there was the smell.

When we left, we felt as though we had spent the evening working inside a burger-and-fries food truck. A nice birthday drink somewhere afterward was no longer particularly appealing. Straight home and into the shower was more realistic.

And that leaves me genuinely puzzled:  Park’s BBQ is hugely popular and, from everything I hear, has been for years. The restaurant was packed. People clearly love it. The portions are generous, the prices are reasonable and the food is good.

My wife and I actually spent much of our 30-minute drive home discussing why this place is so extraordinarily successful. Both of us simply have a hard time believing that all the alternatives are worse.

Perhaps we just value different things in a restaurant experience.

Because while the food itself was good, the combination of the rushed pacing, overwhelming noise and smoke-heavy environment made the entire evening surprisingly underwhelming for me.

And even while writing this, I catch myself wondering whether I somehow need to apologize for giving such a popular restaurant only 2 out of 5 stars, simply because so many other people seem to love it.
But that would defeat the purpose of a review.

I can only rate the experience I actually had — not the rating everyone else has already decided the restaurant deserves.

For years we’ve dined at countless Korean BBQ restaurants across Los Angeles, and for some unknown reason, we somehow managed to skip Park’s BBQ — until now. Maybe it took a special occasion like my brother’s 60th birthday to finally make it happen, and now I’m kicking myself for not taking him here on his 50th!

My wife and I aren’t experts in Korean cuisine, but after many years of dining — including some incredible meals in South Korea — we’re definitely more than casual fans. In our opinion, Park’s just edged out our long-time favorite, Genwa, as the best Korean BBQ in LA.

What sets Park’s apart is the slightly elevated quality of both the meat and the vegetables. And if the measure of great food is how long it lingers in your mind after the meal, Park’s wins by a mile.

The tofu soup had a deep, distinctive flavor with a stronger tofu presence. The steamed egg was thick, silky, and almost tofu-like in texture. Every cut of meat was tender with no aftertaste, and the banchan was flavorful yet surprisingly less salty — I didn’t experience the usual thirst that follows most KBBQ meals.

Reservations? Absolutely essential. Don’t even think about walking in — at 5 p.m. the place was already full.

We’re already planning our return visit, debating what to try next time. But one thing’s for sure: I’m ordering the grilled veggies wrapped in shiso leaf and pickled radish, topped with spicy kimchi — the perfect vegan bite in a meat lover’s paradise.

I honestly had no idea this was a vegan burger place the first couple of times I ate here. I think it was around my third visit when I finally realized everything was plant-based, and I was genuinely shocked. 😂

I’m not vegan or vegetarian, so when I ordered the burger for the first time, I just ate it like a regular burger. The flavor, texture, sauce, and the way everything came together made me think I was eating a normal meat burger. I never stopped to question it.

When I found out it was actually plant-based, I couldn’t believe it. That alone says a lot about how good Monty’s Good Burger is. Usually, you can immediately tell when something is trying to imitate a traditional burger, but that wasn’t my experience here at all. It was satisfying, flavorful, and tasted like an actual indulgent burger rather than a “healthy alternative.”

I’ve been back multiple times now, and the quality has been consistently good. I usually get takeout, and the food still tastes great by the time I get home. The staff has also always been friendly and the service has been quick and easy.

Even if you have absolutely no interest in vegan food, I would still recommend giving this place a try. Don’t go into it thinking, “I’m going to try a vegan burger.” Just order what looks good and judge it as a burger.

The fact that I ate here several times before realizing I wasn’t eating meat is probably the best compliment I can give them. 😂

Definitely one of those places that completely changed my idea of what a plant-based burger can taste like. ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Tiny hole in the wall spot in K Town. Was a top restaurant on Beli and Michelin recommended in 2019, and for good reason.

The restaurant only has 4 items, and we tried 3 out of the 4, enjoying all of them thoroughly.

The Samgyetang was heartwarming with flavours like pine nut, ginseng, and great chicken, and a perfect start to our meal paired with their banchan.

Their Galbijjim was stellar, some of the best I've ever had, more memorable and flavourful than Sun Nong Dan and other Korean spots renowned for 갈비찜. Meat was tender, fatty, and sauces were tasty, yet not overwhelming the flavour of the meat. Additional tteokbokki, potatoes, and other ingredients added great texture as well.

Despite their Galbijjim being immaculate, their Eundaegu-jolim was probably my favourite dish. Reminding me of Chinese style sea bass, the black cod was tender and packed with rich oil and flavour. Something that was truly special and not like anything I had at any other Korean restaurant in LA yet.

Service was also lovely - I felt like I was in a family home, being served the tang into my bowl personally by the owners, and being treated to sliced caracara oranges as dessert.

Will definitely be back!

I asked if he was serious. He looked at me with a smug expression, said, “Nope,” and walked away.

Whether that’s truly the owner’s policy or not, the way it was handled was incredibly rude and unprofessional. One courteous conversation could have left me with a positive impression. Instead, I left feeling disrespected.

It’s unfortunate because they didn’t lose me over the food—they lost me over customer service. This was my first visit, and it will also be my last.

We’ve been coming to this Korean beef soup restaurant in Los Angeles for over 15 years, from when a bowl cost $9 to now around $20, and the quality has never changed.

The aunties working there are very attentive and will regularly check if you need more kimchi or radish, which makes the experience feel very caring and homely.
Parking is relatively easy to find, which is another plus.
The only downside is the restroom. It’s been the same for many years and feels quite old, a bit dirty, and has an unpleasant smell. If they could improve the restroom, it would make the experience much better overall.

Damsot just opened their first U.S. location and I had to experience it for myself — and I’m so glad I did.

This spot is known in Korea for their signature Korean pot rice, and the presentation alone sets the tone. Everything comes out hot, steaming, and full of flavor in a traditional stone pot that really elevates the experience.

As someone who is vegan, I appreciated that there are options that can be modified. I tried the spicy eggplant pot rice and the tofu with shishito peppers — just removing the meat and egg — and both dishes were incredibly satisfying. Rich, comforting, and layered with flavor without feeling like anything was missing.

They also had crispy fried tofu on the side and a smooth drink to finish, which brought everything together perfectly.

The experience felt thoughtful, warm, and elevated. Definitely a place I’ll be coming back to and recommending to anyone looking to explore Korean cuisine in a new way.
